items.title: 68189_Al Hall oral history interview
items.q: The interviewee refers to 'Red Rodneys' in a general sense ('When the Charlie Venturas and Red Rodneys and whatnot started playing...'), indicating awareness of the type of musician rather than a specific personal relationship.

ctx.x: Well, that isn't what they wanted. But naturally, Dick is going to hire all professionals. The band sounded too good, so moving things around -- and so we asked, you know, well, you know, try to get a different sound.

Of course, after, you know, in the days of 52nd Street, and when, you know, the music, despite all the negative criticism began to be -- become the new expression and the new thing of that era, then, of course, I'm not talking about the white musicians who played with these bands like Al Haig and people like that, Red Rodney and what have you, but came behind that when they saw a dollar was to be made with it perhaps. Then white bands started playing in this -- in this style.
You know, they became the so called popularizers, you know, the Charlie Venturas and the George Shearings and, et cetera, et cetera. You know.

items.title: 68189_Al Hall oral history interview
items.q: [INTERVIEWER] ...Red Rodney and what have you... [INTERVIEWEE] Well -- well, let me put it this way. When the Charlie Venturas and Red Rodneys and whatnot started playing with the Black musicians...

ctx.x: You know, they became the so called popularizers, you know, the Charlie Venturas and the George Shearings and, et cetera, et cetera. You know.

Well -- well, let me put it this way. When the Charlie Venturas and Red Rodneys and whatnot started playing with the Black musicians, then if there was a job open, they would become a leader of something important and go from there.
